docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
Welcome to adidas Runtastic Partner API documentation!

The Runtastic Partner API is a REST API. Request and response bodies are, in general, encoded in JSON format. It makes use of standard HTTP status codes and verbs.

All traffic to and from the API must use TLS. This means all API calls must be with the HTTPS scheme. The webhook system also only performs requests through HTTPS. Also, all endpoints require authentication. See the Authentication section for more information.

The base URL for all API endpoints is https://partnerapi.runtastic.com. As the current version of the API is a beta version, the prefix /v0 will be used.

Before jumping in the integration itself, it's recommended that you read some patterns and tools used in the other pages.

Note that we do not provide client libraries for integrating with our API.

docs.title: Support
docs.text: For questions, support or feedback please contact partnerapi.digitalsports@adidas.com.

docs.title: Tools
docs.text: For all the HTTP requests examples, we will use HTTPie. It's a HTTP client with a really intuitive and clean way to write requests, highly recommended.

docs.title: Documentation patterns
docs.text:
In some sections of the documentation, we'll represent placeholders around {}, where the name inside the curly brackets is a variable that would be already received in the presented flow.

The diagram flows use constant arrows to represent requests and dotted arrows to represent responses.

Sync requests will be represented with solid arrowheads and async requests with line arrowheads.

docs.title: Changelog
docs.text: This pages describes relevant changes in the Partner API.
• Changed contact email address to the current one.

• Increased webhook notification delivery attempts
  • Clarified that it is mandatory to revoke all refresh tokens of a user when that user disconnects from adidas running

• Added OAuth scopes pa_activity_write and pa_activity_read to Activity API
  • Deprecated OAuth scope pa_activity for Activity API: Please use pa_activity_write or pa_activity_read instead as specified in the respective endpoint documentation.
• Moved documentation to Stoplight
• Add CRUDI endpoints for receivers GET|POST|PATCH|DELETE /v0/webhooks/receivers
• Updated import activities endpoint to receive param description

docs.title: Initial version
docs.text:
• Features available:

  • Import activities with FIT or GPX files (POST /v0/activities)

  • Retrieve activity (GET /v0/activities/{activity_id})
  • Retrieve GPX trace from activity (GET /v0/activities/{activity_id}/traces/gpx)
  • Create subscription for webhooks (POST /v0/webhooks/subscriptions)

  • Send webhooks to partners when subscribed user creates a new activity

  • Authentication features (OAuth2 flow):

  • Get authorization code from the user

  • Issuing the access token and refresh token through code

  • Issuing access tokens through refresh tokens

  • Global validations:

  • Rate Limiting
  • Request Size Limiting

docs.title: Rate Limiting
docs.text:
The APIs offered by Runtastic in the Partner API have specific rate limits for different time windows that are shared among all the endpoints.

All the endpoints in the Partner API have rate limiting of 10,000 requests per hour and 200 requests per minute. Note that this configuration is per-partner (not per Runtastic user) and can be subject to change without prior notice.

The requests with invalid credentials (expired/invalid access token or invalid authentication key) will not affect the remaining requests of any timeframe.

All the requests successfully authenticated and with valid request size will return HTTP headers representing the maximum requests count and the remaining requests count for each timeframe following the pattern:

X-RateLimit-Limit-{TIMEFRAME}: {MAX}
X-RateLimit-Remaining-{TIMEFRAME}: {REMAINING}

where TIMEFRAME can be: second, minute, hour, day, month and year.

MAX represents the maximum number of requests that can be done in the given TIMEFRAME.

REMAINING represents the number of requests that can still be done inside the given TIMEFRAME.

When one of the limits is reached, a response with 429 status code will be returned with the following format:

HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests
Connection: keep-alive
Content-Length: 37
Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8
Date: Mon, 10 Feb 2020 17:15:55 GMT
Server: kong/1.4.2
X-Kong-Response-Latency: 2
X-RateLimit-Limit-hour: 5
X-RateLimit-Limit-second: 1
X-RateLimit-Remaining-hour: 3
X-RateLimit-Remaining-second: 0

{
    "message": "API rate limit exceeded"
}

It's possible to identify which timeframe limit was reached based on the response headers. In the example above, the value of the header X-RateLimit-Remaining-second is 0.

docs.title: Request Size Limiting
docs.text:
All the APIs will accept requests with maximum body size of 15 Megabytes.

If the request body exceeds this size, the Partner API will return a 413 response, eg:

HTTP/1.1 413 Request Entity Too Large
Connection: keep-alive
Content-Length: 41
Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8
Date: Thu, 12 Mar 2020 14:15:38 GMT
Server: kong/1.3.0.1-enterprise-edition

{
    "message": "Request size limit exceeded"
}

If the request exceeds the maximum size, it won't affect the request rates of the Partner

docs.title: Webhooks
docs.text: Webhooks allow you to be notified of events that occur in Runtastic, like when a user finishes an sport activity.

docs.title: Entities
docs.text:
There are three classes of entities which power the webhooks ecosystem:

  • Receiver
  • Subscription
  • Notification

The next sections describe those entities in detail.

All data representing dates in this document, are based on UTC Timestamps. When being rendered as an HTTP Response, it will be formatted as follows: yyyy-mm-dd hh:mm:ss.

docs.title: Receiver
docs.text:
The Receiver entity holds the URL (also known as the "webhook URL") that will receive POST requests with updates regarding an associated user.

It is possible to have multiple receivers, although having just one should be enough for most use cases. ``yaml json_schema title: Receiver type: object properties: webhook_url: type: string format: uri pattern: ^https example: 'https://www.example.com' description: URL to where the notifications will be sent via HTTPS POST state: type: string enum: - active - deactivated - failure description: Current state of the receiver api_version: type: integer description: API this webhook is using. Currently only0available. example: 0 failure_reason: type: - string - 'null' description: 'When the state of the webhooks isfailure`, this field will contain the reason the webhook failed to be executed.' signing_secret: type: string example: k7xkKLrM1RVjO4G7OgEeAC3OdnBlsxpoCInupCQEBoc= description: Secret used to sign webhook payload. This property will only be returned by the create endpoint! created_at: type: string format: date-time example: '2021-01-14T06:19:41Z' description: Date and time of creation updated_at: type: string format: date-time example: '2021-01-14T06:19:41Z' description: Date and time of the most recent update required: - webhook_url - state - api_version - signing_secret - created_at - updated_at examples: - webhook_url: 'https://www.example.com' state: active api_version: 0 failure_reason: null signing_secret: k7xkKLrM1RVjO4G7OgEeAC3OdnBlsxpoCInupCQEBoc= created_at: '2021-01-14T06:19:41Z' updated_at: '2021-01-14T06:19:41Z'


#### Security considerations

Webhook URLs must be HTTPS. That is, TLS is a must.

TLS version 1.2 or above should be used. Version 1.1 is still allowed, but will be eventually be dropped out. Versions below 1.1 are not allowed and will cause the webhook delivery to fail.

A valid certificate is also required. Self-signed certificates won't be accepted and will cause a webhook delivery to fail.

#### Receivers lifecycle

A receiver is directly related to many notifications, which contain the data that will be sent via POST request to the webhook URL.

<!-- theme: warning -->
>If a notification fails to be delivered multiple times, the associated Receiver will have its state switched to `failure`, which means that new notifications won't be delivered until the Receiver is re-activated. Check [Notifications lifecycle](#notifications-lifecycle).

When a receiver is not active, the associated notifications won't be sent immediately. Once the receiver switches from the `failure` state to the `active` state all the pending notifications **from the last 30 days** will be sent.

It's possible to re-activate a receiver via the [Update Receiver API](../../reference/index.md).

### Subscription

A Subscription binds a list of event types (also known as "topics") from a specific user to a Receiver. A Receiver entity will likely have several Subscription entities bound to it.
</br>
```yaml json_schema
title: Subscription
type: object
properties:
  receiver_id:
    type: string
    format: uuid
    description: The ID of the Receiver bound to this entity
  user_id:
    type: string
    format: uuid
    description: The ID of the user whose events will be listened to
  topics:
    type: array
    description: A set of event types that will trigger this webhook
    items:
      type: string
      example: 'activity:created'
      enum:
        - 'activity:created'
        - 'access_grant:deleted'
  created_at:
    type: string
    format: date-time
    description: Date and time of creation
  updated_at:
    type: string
    format: date-time
    description: Date and time of the most recent update
required:
  - receiver_id
  - user_id
  - topics
  - created_at
  - updated_at
examples:
  - receiver_id: b45de99a-9158-413b-a559-77a398e208f3
    user_id: a169451c-8525-4352-b8ca-070dd449a1a5
    topics:
      - 'activity:created'
    created_at: '2019-08-24T14:15:22Z'
    updated_at: '2019-08-24T14:15:22Z'

Check how to retrieve the user_id when issuing access tokens.

docs.title: Notification
docs.text: Notification is the entity that holds the information that will be sent via webhooks. Besides the payload itself, it also handles how many times it tried to be delivered and also what was the response received from the Receiver URL.

docs.title: Notification delivery
docs.text:
The delivery of a webhook is performed via an HTTP POST request. The usage of TLS with a valid certificate is a must.

Every time an event of type "X" occurs for a user with ID "Y", the webhooks system will match all Subscription entities that contain "X" in the topics attribute and whose user_id attribute equals "Y". For all matches, a Notification entity will be created.

Each Subscription entity fires one webhook with the Notification info for each event that triggered it. An exception to this rule is that when the delivery of the HTTP request fails, it will be retried a few more times, thus generating more requests.

The webhook request must respond with the correct HTTP response code and in a timely manner. If it doesn't, the delivery will be considered unsuccessful. See the Notifications lifecycle section for more information on that and also on how the retry scheme works.

docs.title: Request body
docs.text:
All webhooks carry a payload with a fixed format. The MIME type is always application/json with UTF-8 encoding. The root object is always a JSON object with the following attributes: ```yaml json_schema title: Notification body type: object properties: id: type: string format: uuid example: 5f46acc2-2ee2-44b8-aee1-d8fccb77613f description: The unique identifier for the Notification being delivered occurred_at: type: string description: The timestamp of when the notification was generated format: date-time example: '2021-05-17T09:01:14.000+00:00' topic: type: string enum: - 'activity:created' - 'access_grant:deleted' example: 'activity:created' description: The kind of event that triggered the notification user_id: type: string format: uuid example: dd594643-4aba-4411-92a9-5e5d0fbb3e48 description: The ID of the user associated with this notification data: oneOf: - properties: notification_id: type: string format: uuid example: 2426a1cc-5930-45f7-8345-eba1d4ddb1eb user_id: type: string example: dd594643-4aba-4411-92a9-5e5d0fbb3e48 format: uuid activity_id: type: string format: uuid example: 3f007e97-727a-4eff-aafb-817460055019 description: required if topic is activity:created description: Information that varies accordingly to the given topic type: object required: - id - occurred_at - topic - data examples: - id: 5f46acc2-2ee2-44b8-aee1-d8fccb77613f occurred_at: '2021-05-17T09:01:14.000+00:00' topic: 'activity:created' user_id: dd594643-4aba-4411-92a9-5e5d0fbb3e48 data: notification_id: 2426a1cc-5930-45f7-8345-eba1d4ddb1eb user_id: dd594643-4aba-4411-92a9-5e5d0fbb3e48 activity_id: 3f007e97-727a-4eff-aafb-817460055019


In case of `activity:created` you can fetch the information about the performed activity by extracting the `data.activity_id` and use Get Activity API endpoint to fetch that information.

#### Request headers

The following HTTP headers are sent along in every request:
```yaml json_schema
title: Request headers
type: object
properties:
  Runtastic-Retry-Count:
    type: integer
    minimum: 0
    maximum: 5
    example: 0
    description: It represents how many times this notification failed to be sent
  Runtastic-Api-Version:
    type: integer
    example: 0
    minimum: 0
    description: The API version that was used to create the Subscription
  Runtastic-Signature:
    type: string
    description: The signature to check the authenticity of the request
    example: t=1621242074; sha256=8ea998ab1b348fcdd7878646713a2476442b5121177e1f5529d6b9973a916a6e
required:
  - Runtastic-Retry-Count
  - Runtastic-Api-Version
  - Runtastic-Signature

docs.title: Verifying the request authenticity
docs.text:
To verify the message authenticity, you first have to extract the t and sha256 values off the Runtastic-Signature header of the request.

Runtastic-Signature: t={UNIX_TIMESTAMP}; sha256={SHA256_HMAC_MESSAGE}

t represents the time when the request was made in UTC time (unix timestamp)

sha256 is the result of the SHA-256 HMAC encryption of the webhook payload and the t using the signing_secret from the related Receiver

To perform the verification, you first need to build the payload for the HMAC function. This payload is the concatenation of three components:

  1. The timestamp t
  2. A dot character (.)
  3. The body of the request, untransformed

The calculation of the signature is given by performing a SHA-256 HMAC on the payload described above and using the signing_secret from its Receiver as the key.

docs.title: Mitigate replay attacks
docs.text: You should compare the timestamp value to the current time when you receive the request. If the values differ by more than one minute, the request should be rejected (we suggest returning 403 Forbidden HTTP response for this case).

docs.title: Reject inauthentic webhooks
docs.text: If the received sha256 doesn't match the calculated sha256 message, the request must be rejected (we suggest returning 403 Forbidden HTTP response for this case).

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Let's say that you have a Receiver entity with the following signing_secret:

WBq7ifFlji9TIFuV6cXAnkGSNot5EL9yj2uSzeJF5l3bUhDxo4DNzRZfd8xuWbwo

and you receive the following webhook request:

POST /webhook_endpoint HTTP/1.1
Host: webhooks.example.com
Date: Fri, 06 Dec 2019 09:13:14 -0000
Content-Type: application/json
Content-Length: 19
Runtastic-Retry-Count: 0
Runtastic-Api-Version: 0
Runtastic-Signature: t=1575623594; sha256=813771868026829c936de06d7efdd131eb9f0bab09ae49501d7f8cfdb6da0f24

{"api":"runtastic"}

Extracting the t value from the Runtastic-Signature will give you 1575623594. The payload for the HMAC function will be the following:

1575623594.{"api":"runtastic"}

Supposing the HMAC function signature is HMAC(algorithm, key, payload), it would be called like

HMAC(
  'SHA-256',
  'WBq7ifFlji9TIFuV6cXAnkGSNot5EL9yj2uSzeJF5l3bUhDxo4DNzRZfd8xuWbwo',
  '1575623594.{"api":"runtastic"}'
)

and would return the string

813771868026829c936de06d7efdd131eb9f0bab09ae49501d7f8cfdb6da0f24

which matches the received sha256 from the Runtastic-Signature header.

Then, in this scenario, the request is authentic.

docs.title: Notifications lifecycle
docs.text:
A notification can fail to be delivered due to a few reasons. Among them are DNS failure, TCP/IP failures (connection errors), TLS negotiation failure etc. Those are mostly errors related to the underlying transport mechanism.

Another type of failure is when the webhook request doesn't respond as it should.

All webhook requests must respond in a maximum of 15 seconds with status code 200, 201 or 204. Any other status codes (including 3XX) will be considered a delivery failure.

If you need to perform some processing that could take longer than that, you should perform the processing asynchronously.

In case the delivery fails, due to any reason (e.g. transport failure, wrong status code, request timeout etc), the delivery will be retried.

Each notification will try to be delivered 25 times, with the following interval retry rule (in seconds): (retry_count**4) + 15 + (rand(30) * (retry_count + 1))

If a notification fails to be delivered all the 25 times, the Receiver directly related to it will switch its state to failure, which means that new notifications won't be sent until it is re-activated.

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
Accessing the Runtastic Partner API endpoints requires authentication. This is performed by sending along an access token in the requests following the OAuth2 RFC.

This token can refer only to Partner or to a Partner on behalf of a User.

docs.title: Application credentials
docs.text:
For authentication, you will need a CLIENT_ID along with a corresponding CLIENT_SECRET. You should already have those. If you don't, or if you need assistance with that, you can contact us through partnerapi.digitalsports@adidas.com.

A CLIENT_ID represents an app that interacts with the API. Usually you will have only one, which represents your app. Unless you have more apps, there should be no reason to have more than one CLIENT_ID.

docs.title: Security considerations
docs.text:
The CLIENT_ID can be exposed and shared. However, the CLIENT_SECRET must be kept in secret in a safe place. If someone gets access to the CLIENT_SECRET, they would be able to issue OAuth 2.0 access tokens on behalf of your app.

In case the CLIENT_SECRET gets leaked or stolen, it is very important that you communicate us, preferrably through the partnerapi.digitalsports@adidas.com email address so that we can cancel that secret.

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text: The following flows need to be implemented: * User can connect to adidas running * User can disconnect from adidas running (All refresh tokens of users that disconnect need to be revoked using our API)

docs.title: Partner Authentication
docs.text:
Some entities from the Partner API are not related to an user. The endpoints from these entities won't require the access token from the Partner on behalf of user flow, but one that can be issued only by sending both the CLIENT_ID and the CLIENT_SECRET.

Once you have the access token, you can perform authenticated API requests adding the Authorization header to the requests:

Authorization: Bearer {ACCESS_TOKEN}

docs.title: Issuing an access token
docs.text: The flow to get an access token is pretty straightforward.

docs.title: Endpoint
docs.text: POST https://accounts.runtastic.com/v1/as/token.oauth2

docs.title: Headers
docs.text: Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

docs.title: Body
docs.text: Attribute Type Description client_id String The CLIENT_ID from the Partner client_secret String The CLIENT_SECRET from the Partner grant_type String It must always have the value client_credentials

docs.title: Headers
docs.text: Content-Type: application/json

docs.title: Body
docs.text: Attribute Type Description access_token String 128 characters length expires_in Integer Seconds left to expire the access token token_type String It will always have the value Bearer

docs.title: HTTP Codes
docs.text:
HTTP code Description 200 OK Access Token was issued successfuly

Example:

http -f https://accounts.runtastic.com/v1/as/token.oauth2 \
grant_type=client_credentials \
client_id={CLIENT_ID} \
client_secret={CLIENT_SECRET}

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json;charset=utf-8

{
    "access_token": "XVVM919iy5C4IYuDEweXfrPwR5nKKURkMjkR4ax4C1S0TIeHblE3FthUDtKnimGcUIDkKI1zAW0leWhyVRyOXm7cF8z4Z3mEZvWsTC0tjC9472Z6EnJqgYSy3uGkpfpi",
    "expires_in": 7199,
    "token_type": "Bearer"
}

docs.title: Revoking an access token
docs.text:
Access tokens can be easily revoked. It's advisable to revoke them after usage.

Partner Website->Runtastic Auth Server: Revokes access token
Note right of Partner Website: CLIENT_ID, CLIENT_SECRET, TOKEN
Runtastic Auth Server-->Partner Website: 200 OK

docs.title: Endpoint
docs.text: POST https://accounts.runtastic.com/v1/as/revoke_token.oauth2

docs.title: Headers
docs.text: Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

docs.title: Body
docs.text: Attribute Type Description client_id String The CLIENT_ID from the Partner client_secret String The CLIENT_SECRET from the Partner token String 128 characters long access token

docs.title: Body
docs.text: Empty.

docs.title: HTTP Codes
docs.text:
HTTP code Description 200 OK Access Token was revoked successfuly

Example:

http -f https://accounts.runtastic.com/v1/as/revoke_token.oauth2 \
token={ACCESS_TOKEN} \
client_id={CLIENT_ID} \
client_secret={CLIENT_SECRET}

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html;charset=utf-8

docs.title: Partner in behalf of User Authentication
docs.text: The user's consent is required to access their Runtastic information. To do so, the Authorization Code Grant flow must be implemented from the Partner side.

docs.title: Getting an access token
docs.text:
In order to perform any request to the API, you will need an access token. Remember that all requests from this section are performed in behalf of a Runtastic user and the access token is tied to the user.

There are a few steps for the whole authentication flow. The following sections describe the necessary steps. The following sequence diagram illustrates the whole process:

docs.title: Get authorization from the user
docs.text:
To get the OAuth 2.0 Authorization Code Grant flow started, the first step is to get the user to the following page:

https://accounts.runtastic.com/v1/as/authorization.oauth2
?client_id={CLIENT_ID}
&response_type=code
&scope={SPACE_SEPARATED_SCOPES}
&pfidpadapterid=refid
&redirect_uri={YOUR_APP_CALLBACK_URL}
&state={OPTIONAL_CUSTOM_DATA}

Linebreaks were added for clarity only; that is supposed to be one full URL.

The minimum required scopes are pa_identity and openid plus one of our activity scopes (pa_activity_read or pa_activity_write)

This will likely be a link in your app that will get the user to that URL via a web browser. That page will take care of having the user log in the Runtastic system and display a consent screen asking for permission so that your app may access the user's data. The pieces of data that will be asked for are the ones that you include in the "scope" parameter of the URL above. You should always ask for the most restricted set of scopes that are needed for your app to work. Do not ask for data that won't be used by your app.

Note: The web browser is necessary since OAuth 2.0 is designed with it in mind. There is no way around it.

The placeholders in the query string parameters should be filled in with the appropriate values. The parameters are described as follows:

  • client_id: This must have the client_id that we provided for your app
  • response_type: It must be the string code
  • scope: A list with the scopes the user will give your app consent. The list items are separated by space. Besides pa_identity and openid, which always need to be requested, the following scopes can be used*:
  • pa_activity_read: The user grants your app the permission to read all of the users activities
  • pa_activity_write: The user grants your app the permission to create new activities
  • pfidpadapterid: It must be the string refid
  • redirect_uri: The URL the user will be redirected to when the OAuth flow is finished. See notes below on how to use this parameter
  • state: This parameter is optional. You can send any data here and it will be sent along in the redirect_uri

*If made available to you via our contract

Never send the client_secret value in the URL above, as doing so would publicy expose the secret

Note that the value of the redirect_uri parameter must exactly match one of the URLs you sent us when requesting access to the API. Thus, this value is whitelisted. Also note that you must not include any query string in this URL (i.e. no ? in the URL). Rather than using the query string, you should use the state parameter as it will be appended as a parameter when redirecting the user to the URL in redirect_uri.

In case the user denies access in the consent screen, the redirect to the redirect_uri will still occur. However, the code parameter will not be included and instead, the parameters error_description and error will be set. The value of error will be access_denied, and error_description will include a textual description of the error.

docs.title: Do not use webviews
docs.text: Webviews block pop-ups, meaning that users that use social logins (Google / Apple / Facebook) won't be able to login as the pop-up to enter credentials will not be shown. Thus always open the flow in the users native browser.

docs.title: Issuing the access token and refresh token
docs.text:
When the OAuth flow is finished and consent has been successfully granted, the user will be redirected, in the web browser, to the URL you provided in the redirect_uri parameter in the URL above. The redirect will add a query string parameter named code that will be exchanged for the access token and refresh token.

If you sent a state attribute to the authorization URL, it will be sent along with the same name, as a query parameter, in this redirect. Its value is left untouched and it is opaque to us, so the value you provided won't be modified in any way.

The backend behind the redirect_uri must be under your control. It must immediately exchange the authorization code (that is, the code parameter) with the access token by performing a POST HTTP request to the URL https://accounts.runtastic.com/v1/as/token.oauth2.

The contents of the request must be encoded as in the application/x-www-form-urlencoded MIME type (see more).

The parameters to be sent in the body are the following:

  • grant_type: It must be the string authorization_code
  • client_id: The client_id of your app
  • client_secret: The client_secret of your app
  • code: The authorization code you received in the redirect URL
  • redirect_uri: The redirect_uri that you used in the authorization URL (the one in the first step of the OAuth flow)

This call must be performed from the server side, never from a web browser or mobile client, as that would expose the client_secret value.

The response will be a JSON encoded object. An example response is as follows:

{
  "access_token": "sbfWbvBnG8jhbYBt1eJAoi",
  "refresh_token": "3yDbEc22RjJDBTJHwMnyPFwFzVOqjKq4V0A47RwhwdRjkdJFFkLI2E9GtbBmHzqm2MlhJZmf4B4RIJTnaGLWLn2SZSzKx0c2Px7Qb5iW0txIPhGcRV2elF7IZtn6jMzr",
  "token_type": "Bearer",
  "expires_in": 7199
}

The access_token and refresh_token attributes contain the access and refresh tokens, respectively. You must store these in a safe place and they must never be shared. The expires_in attribute tells how long, in seconds, until the access token expires. In the example above, it is valid within the next 120 minutes from when the request was performed.

It can also be that the response includes an id_token attribute. Its content is a JWT which includes information regarding the user. The sub claim of the JWT corresponds to the user ID. The user ID is useful to identify the user when receiving webhooks.

At this point you can already perform API calls using the access token.

See the following sections for information on how to use the access token and how the expiry time and refresh tokens should be dealt with.

docs.title: OpenID scope
docs.text:
In order to retrieve information from the user associated with the access token, the scope openid must be added in the SPACE_SEPARATED_SCOPES.

If that's done, the requests to issue access tokens will return the attribute id_token, which is a JWT with information regarding the user in its payload, eg.:

{
    "access_token": "DAwD8r2mL91Z7J6aAp9JFEHj9QWVWJq02k4OtdSjd35adrLM8aD20Fl0xAazwg7SsIabdqQC1lzHGWVFGMyhp7tVgSbUnKKe8sWDrfvqo0JYZQwqYdZMB4qRNZzdOBtR",
    "refresh_token": "23DF5LuLI5WGyo9zoRM5Jy7ONx9Rk0BZiHFW317AIKFoD3RhbSkdo1aXJiQ36ZCCbmU0waufafOl2pVTMwOwxDL201eE7n91jBO0HlTVKAuSwmIVxmNwoueLDE02AsaD",
    "id_token": "eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIsImtpZCI6IjZwaE9YTHFqVU42RHBBck9iUmRSSVcifQ.eyJpc3MiOiJodHRwczovL2FjY291bnRzLnJ1bnRhc3RpYy5jb20vdjEiLCJpYXQiOjE2MTU5MTA2OTUsImV4cCI6MTY0NzQ0NjY5NSwiYXVkIjoicGFwaV9wYXJ0bmVyIiwic3ViIjoiQUxEQzRNTjEyRURBQjlHSCJ9.h3RoExoZgwCQO16QUJFGaG9GluRXxuuDGBayHkb3gDoofoxYib3HKBPuJR-oTl-3AlzgpgpZsbHkaCPvRD0Pu5Q2se4yUlE7MrMKKbccrS6COlEe3laQNsgZDXMXCY3Aq4GAgUYjzXE2-2FaLw1eQu1anSahKiiW4z7R0nAmjoTwfwhIVSg6d0ourNAOcs5XhIz8f-ahNu8A2PXQvx2sbGQPKdMSeeA05f_1f-7nDXKEpIrW9qAdgwFNw-4nnk_fl1Nqq6Qni4D6XIcZAdIDT6dnP_uNVMAInAnqAJcDtT8bIxxfUjjq7N13jUXsbJfe8-5tu7ko_HMu3yM6TZr_cA",
    "token_type": "Bearer",
    "expires_in": 899

The decoded JWT payload results in:

{
  "sub": "ALDC4MN12EDAB9GH",
  "aud": "papi_partner",
  "jti": "eEym4uPLXgcF9F3p5lGc4f",
  "iss": "https://accounts.runtastic.com/v1",
  "iat": 1615897609,
  "exp": 1615897909
}

The sub attribute represents the user_id.

docs.title: Issuing access tokens through refresh tokens
docs.text:
The section above demonstrates how to issue an access token given that you have the authorization code. This section extends that one, but applies to the case where you don't have the authorization code anymore (since it is used only once) and want to issue a new access token.

To perform that, the same rules as for the previous section apply. That is the same URL (https://accounts.runtastic.com/v1/as/token.oauth2) and format is to be used here.

What is changed is the body payload. In this case, the authentication itself occurs with the refresh token rather than the authorization code. The body payload for the HTTP request takes the following attributes:

  • grant_type: Its value must be the string refresh_token
  • client_id: The client_id of your app
  • client_secret: The client_secret of your app
  • refresh_token: The refresh token that you previously received
  • redirect_uri: The redirect_uri that you used in the authorization URL (the one in the first step of the OAuth flow)

The response payload will look like the following:

{
  "access_token": "3ShyuHkKPsWUFRMZlgwFq4",
  "token_type": "Bearer",
  "expires_in": 7199
}

docs.title: Performing authenticated API requests
docs.text:
Once you have the access token, you can perform authenticated API requests.

Just add the Authorization header to every API request. It takes the following form:

Authorization: Bearer {ACCESS_TOKEN}

For instance, if your access token is sbfWbvBnG8jhbYBt1eJAoi, then just add the following header to your requests:

Authorization: Bearer sbfWbvBnG8jhbYBt1eJAoi

Although the authentication is very simple, there are a few gotchas due to the fact that OAuth 2.0 access tokens have an expiry time. Please see the next section for more details on how to handle expired access tokens and best practices.

docs.title: Revoking a token
docs.text:
It is possible to revoke a token, be it a refresh token or an access token. The revocation endpoint is implemented as specified in RFC 7009. It is located at https://accounts.runtastic.com/v1/as/revoke_token.oauth2.

In the case that the user requests that their account gets disconnected from adidas runtastic, it is mandatory that you call this endpoint to revoke all refresh tokens of this user.

The contents of the request must be encoded as in the application/x-www-form-urlencoded MIME type.

When a refresh token is revoked, all access tokens issued by it are automatically revoked as well.

To revoke a token, just issue a POST request to that endpoint passing in the following parameters:

  • client_id: The client_id of your app
  • client_secret: The client_secret of your app
  • token: The token to be revoked

On success, the response will have an empty body with a 200 status code.

docs.title: Access token best practices
docs.text: Since OAuth 2.0 is rather complex, due to the inherent complexity of having a secure software system, this section aims to avoid issues when dealing with access token expiry times and refresh tokens.

docs.title: Access token expiration
docs.text:
Access tokens will have a short expiration time. Usually not more than a few hours. Once an access token is expired, calling the API with it will yield the same results as calling it with an invalid token. That is because the token has, in fact, been invalidated.

The access token may also expire before its expiry date. However, that should be considered an edge case and unlikely to happen often.

See the "handling expired tokens" section below on how to handle token expiration.

docs.title: Refresh token expiration
docs.text:
The refresh token does not expire.

In general, this means the refresh token does not change. However, it can be revoked if it gets compromised (see revoking a token).

docs.title: Handling expired tokens
docs.text:
An API call with an invalid or expired access token will result in a "401 Unauthorized" response with the following JSON body payload:

{
  "error": "invalid_token",
  "error_description": "The access token is invalid or has expired"
}

Your app must be prepared to handle expired access tokens at any time. In order to recover from an expired access token, your app has to request a new access token by using the refresh token. Remember that the refresh token does not expire. See section Issuing access tokens through refresh tokens for how to issue a new access token using the refresh token.

It is possible to have more than one valid access token at the same time. This fact should make it easier to manage the access token. However, your app must not issue access tokens without any form of control in place, as that could negatively impact our infrastructure. For instance, the app should not issue a new access token at the very beginning of an operation and then discard it after the operation has finished.

Your app must not issue access tokens without any form of control in place.

Your app should try and keep only one valid access token at a time. Although this is not a strict requirement, it should be done in a best effort manner.

docs.title: OpenAPI source maintenance
docs.text: The files under openapi/source are the maintained API contract. Run ruby bin/generate_oas.rb after editing them. Do not edit openapi/generated/partner-api.v0.yaml directly.

docs.title: Migration provenance
docs.text:
The initial endpoint contract and models came from the committed runpapi-public-api-docs/reference/partners.v0.yaml reference. The older runpapi-partner-api-openapi specification was used to compare endpoint coverage and recover shared response and pagination shapes. Neither original folder is needed to generate or serve this documentation.

The former public reference depended on unavailable service repositories and remote Stoplight schemas. The local bad-request, not-found, conflict, unauthorized, rate-limit, request-size-limit, pagination, and links schemas were reconstructed from committed examples and the older local shared components. Review these local schemas against authoritative service contracts when those sources become available.

docs.title: Source layout
docs.text:
• openapi/source/base.yaml: API metadata and server information.
  • openapi/source/paths: activity and webhook operations.
  • openapi/source/components/common.yaml: parameters, headers, security schemes, and reusable responses.
  • openapi/source/models: API resource, request, and response schemas.
  • openapi/source/schemas: reconstructed shared error and JSON:API schemas.
  • openapi/source/manifest.yaml: deterministic assembly order.

The generator rejects duplicate paths and components, external references, unresolved sources, and unexpected path or operation counts.

docs.title: API reference
docs.text:
Open the interactive Partner API reference in Swagger Editor.

The Partner API endpoints use version v0. Authentication is provided by the version v1 account service, so the authentication guide remains under authentication/v1.
